name: Polynesian himene tarava (Tahitian / Cook-Island congregational polyphony)
lineage: Tahitian and Cook-Island congregational polyphonic Christian-hymn tradition that emerged through the post-1797 London Missionary Society Protestant evangelization of French Polynesia — fusing pre-contact Polynesian vocal practice with Western hymn-text structure; the canonical himene tarava is a three-or-more-voice unaccompanied congregational form sung by maohi communities across Tahiti, Moorea, Raiatea, and the Cook Islands, with named voice-parts including the marû (high female voice carrying ornament), the tahito (text-leading voice), the haamana (bass anchor), and the falsetto-break leo-kiekie octave-leap as a deliberate ornament-figure; parallel forms include Tahitian aparima (sung-with-gesture form), ute (humorous improvisational form), and Cook-Island ute and akaau congregational hymns; preserved through annual Heiva i Tahiti festival competition and the Cook Islands National Arts Theatre cultural-preservation infrastructure
